input:
I believe teenagers should not hold regular jobs while they are full-time students. A job may provide experience and money, but those benefits do not outweigh its pressure.
Employment can harm a student's physical and mental health. School already requires long hours of homework, revision, and exam preparation. Students often need evenings to finish assignments or recover from a demanding day. A regular job adds fixed responsibilities when students most need flexibility. Workers must arrive on time, cover shifts, and sometimes stay late when a workplace is busy. Going directly from school to work often cuts into sleep, exercise, and proper meals. A student finishing a late shift may still have homework and may not sleep until after midnight. Repeated nights like this can cause exhaustion, stress, and poor concentration the next day. Thus, job pressure can gradually damage both health and school life.
Paid work can also distract teenagers from their academic goals. Earning money gives an immediate reward, while the benefits of studying can seem distant. An extra shift may therefore feel more attractive than preparing for a test or difficult project. Work schedules can also conflict directly with school responsibilities. Even two weekday shifts can remove hours needed for reading, group work, or teacher help. Fatigue and poor preparation can then reduce a student's classroom performance. I have seen classmates arrive after late shifts and struggle to stay awake during lessons. If lower grades continue, a teenager may lose confidence in education and value income more. In an extreme case, steady earnings may even encourage a student to leave education too early.
Teenage employment can also take away experiences that belong to a limited stage of life. Friendships, clubs, sports, family activities, and free time are not merely entertainment. These experiences teach teamwork, reveal interests, and build lasting relationships. A teenager who repeatedly misses activities for work may lose friends or abandon a valued hobby. Adolescence should include time for rest, social development, and personal growth. Adults have many years to work, but a missed school trip or close friendship cannot be recreated later.
Supporters often argue that teenage jobs teach responsibility and independence. However, volunteering, school projects, household duties, and holiday work can teach similar lessons without a weekly job. These alternatives provide useful experience while keeping the school term centered on education.
For these reasons, teenagers should focus on studies and personal growth rather than regular jobs during the school year. Protecting their health, academic attention, and irreplaceable youth gives them a stronger foundation for work later.

Closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras are now common in schools, shops, offices, and many other premises. Even so, I believe CCTV cameras should be installed in workplaces and other premises where theft or threats to people are realistic concerns. Their value in preventing crime and protecting employees is greater than the loss of some privacy.

First, CCTV can reduce theft and make it easier to deal with crimes that still occur. Visible cameras discourage some people from stealing because they know that their actions may be recorded. For example, an employee who is considering taking money from a counter may think again if a camera clearly covers that area. Cameras also create useful evidence after a robbery has happened. Clear footage can show a suspect's appearance, movements, or vehicle and give police information that witnesses may have missed. In Malaysia, for instance, police have used CCTV recordings to trace and arrest thieves after a Seven Eleven store was broken into at night. A recording can also help managers distinguish between an actual theft and a simple mistake involving stock or cash. Therefore, workplaces with CCTV are better equipped both to discourage theft and to identify those responsible when prevention fails.

CCTV can also protect employees who have to deal directly with angry or distressed customers. Workers in shops, reception areas, restaurants, and service counters cannot always avoid confrontations. A customer who knows that an interaction is being recorded may be less willing to threaten, strike, or falsely accuse an employee. This awareness can calm some disputes before they become dangerous. If an incident does become serious, the recording provides a neutral account of what happened. It can show who began the confrontation and whether an employee followed workplace rules. Such evidence protects workers from both physical danger and unfair blame. It also allows an employer to improve safety procedures after reviewing how an incident developed. For these reasons, CCTV offers employees practical protection when personal testimony alone may be disputed.

Cameras can also help a workplace respond more quickly to suspicious behavior. Staff cannot watch every entrance, corridor, storage room, or parking area at the same time. A monitored camera system can reveal unusual activity in a place that is temporarily unattended. Security staff can then investigate before the situation becomes a larger loss or a threat to workers. This is particularly useful at night or in large premises with few employees present.

Critics therefore argue that CCTV should not be widely installed because constant surveillance can interfere with privacy. Employees should not feel that every harmless conversation or movement is being examined without reason. However, this concern does not mean that CCTV should be rejected entirely. Cameras can be limited to security-sensitive common areas such as entrances, sales floors, counters, and storage spaces instead of private places such as toilets or changing rooms. Employers should also explain why cameras are present and restrict access to recordings. With these limits, a workplace can protect reasonable privacy while preserving evidence needed for safety. Where theft and confrontations are genuine risks, preventing serious harm should take priority over the smaller privacy cost of properly controlled surveillance.

In conclusion, CCTV cameras are an important security measure and should be installed in workplaces and other premises where people or property need protection. They can discourage theft, provide useful evidence, protect employees during customer conflicts, and help staff notice danger sooner. Although surveillance creates legitimate privacy concerns, sensible limits on camera placement and recording access can reduce those concerns. Overall, the protection CCTV provides against thieves, intruders, and dangerous incidents makes it a necessary safeguard.

Growing populations and endangered species often compete for the same limited land. Protecting wildlife is important, but I believe essential human needs should receive higher priority when land is scarce.

First, population growth increases the demand for food. Farmers need land to grow wheat, corn, vegetables, and other crops. If productive land is unavailable while communities lack food, families can face shortages and higher prices. Farmland is therefore essential to human survival. Cultivation near growing towns can supply local markets and reduce dependence on distant food sources.

Second, people need land for safe housing. A town cannot fit more families into the same number of homes forever. Without new residential areas, overcrowding may increase and poorer families may be pushed into unsafe buildings. Land for housing therefore protects health as well as comfort. Proper homes also shelter people from severe weather and give children a stable place to sleep and study.

Land is also needed for industries and public facilities. Hospitals, medicine factories, water-treatment plants, and warehouses all require physical space. A medicine factory may occupy land, but its products can protect thousands of people from disease. Industrial development can also create jobs that help families pay for food and housing. Some land must therefore be available for necessary industry and services.

Some people argue that endangered species should always receive land first because extinction is permanent. Governments should avoid destroying habitats unnecessarily. However, wildlife protection does not require treating every piece of land as untouchable. Authorities can protect important habitats and direct farms or housing toward less sensitive areas. This can preserve species while still meeting urgent human needs.

In conclusion, endangered plants and animals deserve protection, but the needs of a growing human population should come first when a direct choice must be made. People need land for agriculture, housing, industry, and essential services because these uses directly affect survival and security. The best approach is to protect wildlife intelligently while giving priority to the land people genuinely need to build stable lives.

Choosing a career is one of the most important decisions a young person makes. Personally, I believe choosing a career similar to one's parents can improve a person's professional journey because parents can provide knowledge, advice, and useful connections.

To begin with, parents who work in the same field can give their children specialized guidance from experience. They have already faced many problems that beginners are likely to meet. My father, for example, is a software engineer, and his experience has helped me understand programming and computer science more quickly. When I get stuck on a programming problem, I can ask him how he would approach it instead of spending hours guessing at solutions. His advice helps me understand why a method fails and how to find a better one. This saves time and lets me learn from mistakes he made earlier in his career. It also gives me an advantage over classmates who may have to find this information alone. If I had chosen a field completely different from my father's, I would probably face more uncertainty and have fewer people at home who could answer detailed questions.

Another advantage is that parents who have spent many years in an industry usually understand how that industry works. Over time, they often build professional networks and learn which employers have good reputations. They may know which companies offer strong training programs or good opportunities for advancement. This knowledge can help a young person avoid applying blindly to unsuitable positions. Parents may also know colleagues who can describe workplaces or recommend a promising applicant. A recommendation from a respected professional can make an application more convincing. A candidate with a credible recommendation may receive serious attention earlier in the hiring process. Such connections should not replace ability, but they can help a qualified beginner get a chance to demonstrate it.

Parents in the same profession can also give realistic advice about long-term career development. An experienced worker knows the daily pressures, required skills, and possible routes for promotion. This can help a young person decide whether the career truly matches his or her interests before investing years in training.

Critics may argue that following a parent's profession is risky because the job market changes rapidly. New technology can reduce demand for some occupations and create new ones. I agree that young people should not copy their parents' choices without thinking. However, uncertainty about future trends does not make parental experience useless. No one can predict which career will remain popular for the next thirty years. An experienced parent can still help a child identify transferable skills and adapt when conditions shift. Therefore, the sensible choice is not to follow a parent's career automatically, but to use the parent's knowledge when the field also suits the child's abilities and interests.

In conclusion, choosing a career similar to one's parents can provide valuable support throughout a professional journey. Parents can share specialized knowledge, offer realistic information about employers, and introduce useful professional contacts. Although the future job market is uncertain, that uncertainty affects every career choice. In my view, when a young person is genuinely interested in the same field, parental guidance can lead him or her toward a more favorable career trajectory.

Whether wealthy countries should help poorer nations improve their infrastructure is debated. I believe affluent nations are justified in sharing part of their wealth with less privileged countries.

From an ethical perspective, ignoring severe suffering when help is possible is difficult to defend. People in poorer countries may lack clean water, hospitals, safe roads, or enough food even though richer states can help. A new water system, for example, can prevent disease in a community. Wealthy countries can support such projects without reducing their own living standards. Compassion is promoted by many religions, including Buddhism and Islam. Prosperous nations should therefore help people whose basic needs cannot be met without outside assistance.

There is also an economic reason for providing aid because cooperation can benefit both sides. Developing countries gain immediately when assistance helps build roads, schools, hospitals, and communication networks. Better infrastructure helps local businesses operate and gives people greater access to education, health care, and employment. Developed countries can also gain knowledge through such cooperation. Medical teams working in poorer regions may encounter diseases that require new research. Research into these challenges can improve medicines and strengthen the pharmaceutical sector of the assisting country.

Economic cooperation can also create markets. Many developing nations have large populations whose purchasing power may rise as their economies grow. By helping these countries develop and maintaining good relations, wealthy nations can build trust with future trading partners. Their companies may later find new markets for technology, medicine, and machinery. Developing countries can also sell agricultural goods, minerals, and raw materials to their partners at competitive prices. These exchanges can support economic growth on both sides rather than making assistance a one-way loss.

Aid should be carefully managed so that money is not wasted or misused. However, the risk of poor management is a reason to supervise projects and demand transparency, not a reason to refuse all assistance.

In conclusion, assistance from wealthy countries is not only an ethical act but also a sensible long-term investment that can yield benefits for both sides. It can reduce suffering, improve infrastructure, encourage useful research, and create stronger trading relationships. Nations that show empathy toward less fortunate people while building fair partnerships are more likely to earn trust and achieve lasting success.

University classes are important, but they are not the only way students can learn. In my view, attending classes should be a choice for students rather than a compulsory requirement.

To begin with, some university students can gain a deeper understanding from resources outside the classroom. A student who already understands a lecture topic may learn more by studying independently in the library. There, the student can spend extra time on difficult chapters instead of reviewing familiar material. Textbooks, academic articles, and discussions with classmates can also explain a topic from different perspectives. A close friend of mine studied in the same department as I did and usually understood class material very quickly. She seldom attended lectures that repeated material she had mastered and instead used those hours to work on difficult topics by herself. Because she studied seriously, she eventually graduated with excellent grades. Her experience shows that absence from a classroom does not necessarily mean absence from learning.

Students should also be free to use class time for other beneficial academic activities when they already have a strong grasp of the course material. Research projects and practical work can develop skills that lectures may not provide. In my own case, I often skipped biology classes because attendance was not compulsory and I had already studied most biology topics before entering university. I used those hours to work on my chemistry research instead. The extra time allowed me to read more papers and improve my project. At the end of the course, I earned an A+ in both biology and chemistry. For a prepared student, flexible attendance can therefore make study time more productive.

Optional attendance requires students to act responsibly. Some students may skip classes simply because they do not feel like studying, and their grades may suffer. However, this risk does not justify forcing every student to attend every lecture. University students should learn to judge which activities deserve their time and accept the consequences of poor choices. Giving them this responsibility can also teach time management.

In summary, students should be allowed to decide whether attending a particular university class is the best use of their time. Independent study can sometimes provide deeper learning, while flexible schedules can allow well-prepared students to pursue valuable academic work. Therefore, attendance at university should not be compulsory, provided that students remain responsible for mastering the course requirements.

Television and films are a major part of modern entertainment and clearly influence the way people think and act. Although they can provide relaxation and information, I believe television and movies generally have a more negative than positive influence on our behavior. They encourage unhealthy eating, reduce interaction with loved ones, and pressure viewers to imitate unrealistic or harmful images.

One negative effect is that television can encourage unhealthy eating habits. Many people automatically snack while watching because eating becomes part of the viewing routine. When viewers focus on a screen, they may pay less attention to how much they consume. These snacks are often chips, pizza, sweets, or sugary drinks rather than healthy food. Television advertising makes the problem worse by repeatedly presenting fast food in attractive ways. A child who sees the same pizza advertisement several times may begin asking for it even when not hungry. Frequent consumption of these foods can contribute to weight gain and obesity-related illnesses.

Television and films can also reduce communication with family and friends. Children who spend several hours in front of a screen have fewer opportunities to talk with their parents about school or daily experiences. Even when a family watches a film together, everyone usually pays attention to the screen instead of speaking. By contrast, board games or shared meals naturally require conversation. If screen entertainment repeatedly replaces these activities, family members may know less about one another's lives. Over time, this can weaken close relationships.

Another problem is that television, films, and advertisements can make viewers dissatisfied with themselves and encourage imitation. Advertisements often present attractive models and carefully edited bodies as if they were normal. Viewers who compare themselves with these images may feel inadequate about their own appearance. Some then spend heavily on beauty products or gym memberships because they feel pressure to look like people on screen. Movies can have a similar effect when admired characters make risky behavior look fashionable. If a popular character smokes and appears confident, young fans may associate smoking with that image. A teenager may copy the behavior even without truly wanting to smoke.

Of course, television and films can provide entertainment, education, and relaxation. However, these benefits do not require people to watch for many hours or accept every message they see. People can enjoy media in moderation while remaining critical of advertisements and fictional behavior.

In conclusion, television and films are entertaining, but their overall influence on behavior is often negative. Unhealthy eating, reduced communication, insecurity about appearance, and imitation of harmful habits are serious consequences. To protect their health, relationships, and sense of identity, people should reduce unnecessary screen time and choose carefully what they allow these media to influence.

Trying unfamiliar activities can reveal hidden talents and teach us about ourselves. However, time is limited, and chasing things we are not good at can make us overlook areas where we could achieve more. Therefore, I firmly believe that people should concentrate mainly on their strengths.

First, focusing on a strength makes it easier to achieve ambitious goals. Real success usually requires years of repeated practice rather than occasional effort in many unrelated areas. When a person already has ability in a field, each additional hour of practice can build on skills that are already developed. This creates steady progress and allows the person to tackle increasingly difficult problems. Albert Einstein, for example, devoted most of his professional life to physics and became famous for major contributions such as the theories of special and general relativity. He did not become successful by trying to master every possible subject equally. His example suggests that concentrating effort in a field of strong ability can produce exceptional results.

Second, working on strengths can turn natural ability into a much higher level of skill. People often enjoy activities in which they can see themselves improving. That satisfaction increases interest and makes regular practice easier to continue. In junior high school, mathematics was the subject in which I performed best. Because solving difficult problems gave me a strong sense of achievement, I began studying questions beyond what our teacher required. I gradually moved from ordinary school exercises to much more advanced problems. As a result, my test scores improved and I was eventually able to solve some problems at university level. This experience taught me that a strength becomes much more valuable when it is developed deliberately.

Focusing on strengths can also help people use limited opportunities wisely. A student may have only a few free hours each day after classes and other responsibilities. If those hours are divided among many activities in which the student has little interest or ability, progress in each one may remain small. Spending most of that time on a promising strength can instead create expertise that leads to competitions, scholarships, or future career opportunities. Of course, exploring new interests still has value. However, exploration should not repeatedly take time away from abilities that are already producing meaningful progress.

In conclusion, concentrating on existing strengths gives people a better chance to reach important goals and improve their abilities to a high level. New experiences can still be useful, but they should not distract us from developing the talents in which we have the greatest potential. Honing our strongest skills is therefore a practical path toward significant achievement and long-term improvement.

Technological progress has changed almost every part of modern life. Some people argue that these changes create more problems than benefits. Personally, I disagree and believe technology has made human life better overall, although its harmful effects should be controlled carefully.

First, modern technology has greatly improved convenience and efficiency. Many modern devices reduce the time and effort required for ordinary tasks. A washing machine, for example, lets a family clean clothes while using the same time for work, study, or rest. Computers and smartphones also allow people to communicate and find information within minutes. Together, these inventions give people more time for productive activities.

Technology has also made an important contribution to medicine. Modern equipment allows doctors to detect illnesses earlier and monitor patients more accurately. Detailed scans, for example, may reveal internal problems that are difficult to identify through observation alone. Earlier diagnosis gives doctors a better chance to treat a disease before it becomes severe. Technological progress can therefore directly protect health and save lives.

At the same time, technological development has real disadvantages. Producing electronic devices can damage the natural environment because factories require metals, fuels, water, and energy. Mining raw materials may destroy habitats, while manufacturing can create pollution. Frequently replacing phones and computers also produces electronic waste. These costs show that technological progress should be managed responsibly rather than accepted without limits.

Another concern is that excessive dependence on technology may reduce creativity, particularly among children and young people. If students immediately search online for every answer, they may spend less time solving problems independently. Creative ability often develops when people experiment, make mistakes, and think through difficulties for themselves. Young people should therefore use technology as a tool rather than allowing it to replace independent thought.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that technology contributes greatly to human life and the advancement of civilization. It saves time, increases convenience, and plays a crucial role in modern medicine. Its environmental and creative costs are serious, but they are reasons for wiser use rather than reasons to reject technological progress. Overall, society should continue developing useful technology while controlling the damage it can cause.

Art can influence how people think, so some people believe governments should restrict what artists are allowed to express. I believe artists should generally be free to create and communicate their ideas, because excessive restrictions weaken creativity and freedom of expression, although artists should still act responsibly when their work could cause serious social harm.

The first reason for protecting artistic freedom is that creativity develops best when artists can explore unusual ideas. Strict rules can make artists avoid original subjects because they fear punishment by authorities. When creators constantly ask whether an idea is officially acceptable, they are more likely to repeat safe and familiar patterns. By contrast, freedom encourages experimentation with new styles and stories. The lasting popularity of works by Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo shows how strongly societies value bold imagination. Great art often comes from people who are willing to think differently from those around them. Therefore, broad restrictions on artistic ideas can reduce the chance that remarkable and innovative works will be produced.

Artistic freedom is also connected to the basic right to express opinions. In a democratic society, citizens should be able to discuss social problems and question public institutions without unnecessary interference. Art provides a powerful way to do this because stories can make abstract problems understandable through individual experiences. The film '3 Idiots', for example, criticizes an education system that emphasizes memorization and examinations instead of practical understanding. Viewers can enjoy the story while also considering whether schools place unhealthy pressure on students. If governments prevent artists from raising uncomfortable questions, society may lose an important source of criticism and discussion. Denying artists reasonable freedom of expression can therefore weaken both individual rights and public debate.

However, complete freedom can create genuine difficulties when artistic work deals carelessly with highly sensitive issues. In a multicultural country such as Malaysia, irresponsible portrayals of ethnic or religious groups could offend communities and increase tension. A film that deliberately spreads hatred against one group can affect people far beyond the cinema. Governments therefore have a legitimate interest in preventing direct incitement to violence or similarly serious harm. Some might therefore argue that governments need broad restrictions on artistic expression. Yet this danger does not justify broad censorship of controversial ideas. Most artists understand that damaging their reputation or provoking needless hostility can also harm their careers. Public criticism and narrowly focused laws against direct harm can discourage reckless expression without controlling ordinary artistic opinions. A society can protect public safety while still leaving artists substantial room to create freely.

In conclusion, the possible misuse of artistic freedom should be taken seriously, but it should not become an excuse for governments to control artistic creation in general. Freedom allows artists to develop original work, express social concerns, and encourage citizens to think about important issues. Although limited rules may be justified when expression directly promotes serious harm, artists should not face broad limitations merely because their ideas are unconventional or critical. Memorable and captivating art depends greatly on the liberty to imagine, question, and express.

Living with a roommate is important because two people must share space and routines. From my perspective, the most important quality of a good roommate is consideration. Effective communication is equally essential because even considerate people can misunderstand each other.

Being considerate makes life more comfortable and prevents unnecessary conflict. Roommates share limited space, so one person's habits can easily affect the other person. For example, a considerate roommate lowers the volume of music or television late at night. This matters when the other student needs to sleep or prepare for an exam. A considerate person also keeps common areas clean and avoids using another person's belongings without permission. These habits show respect for another person's needs. Consideration can therefore support a student's academic life as well as the roommate relationship. A quiet and respectful room gives both students a better place to rest and study.

Communication is another vital characteristic of a good roommate. People grow up with different habits and may have different ideas about what is normal. One student may make the bed every morning, while another may not consider that task important. Problems become worse when roommates assume that their own habits are the only reasonable ones. Discussing expectations early can prevent differences from being interpreted as laziness or disrespect. For instance, roommates can agree on quiet hours, cleaning duties, visitors, and shared items. If one person is unhappy, calmly explaining the problem is usually better than suddenly deciding to move out. Effective communication therefore eliminates misunderstandings and makes compromise possible.

Consideration and communication also help people adapt to different personalities. It is unrealistic to expect a roommate to behave exactly as we want. University brings together people from different families and backgrounds, so some differences are unavoidable. A student who listens, explains personal needs, and accepts reasonable compromises learns social skills.

To sum up, consideration and communication are the most essential qualities of a good roommate. Consideration encourages respect for another person's comfort and study, while communication helps roommates solve differences before they become major conflicts. We cannot always choose a person whose habits perfectly match our own. A successful roommate relationship depends on respecting differences, discussing problems honestly, and adapting when necessary.

University professors are responsible for educating students, but universities also depend on them to create new knowledge. I believe professors should devote more time to research than to classroom teaching, as long as they still fulfill basic teaching duties.

First, active research helps professors remain specialists in their fields. Knowledge changes quickly, especially in science and technology, so relying only on old material can make expertise outdated. Reading new studies and testing ideas keep professors intellectually active. This can also improve teaching because professors can connect textbook concepts with current work. The most memorable professor from my university experience was Mr. Yang, who constantly read papers and conducted research. He often used examples from his projects to explain difficult ideas. His lessons felt more meaningful, and he taught us how to study independently. My classmates regarded him as an outstanding educator.

Research-active professors also give students opportunities that books and ordinary lectures cannot provide. Students can learn basic knowledge from textbooks, online resources, and classroom instruction. However, students who want to join real research need guidance from someone who understands how projects are designed. A professor who is not doing research may struggle to offer meaningful projects. By contrast, an active researcher can invite students to collect data, test an idea, or discuss a new method. These experiences teach students how knowledge is produced instead of merely memorized. Research discussions may also encourage students to suggest original ideas that improve a project.

University research also benefits society beyond the campus. Professors contribute to scientific, artistic, and cultural fields. Their investigations can lead to new technologies and medical methods that improve people's lives. Research in conservation can help preserve artworks and historical objects before they are permanently damaged. Scholars in history and archaeology can deepen our understanding of earlier generations. If professors spent nearly all their time repeating established knowledge in classrooms, society would lose much of this discovery and preservation work.

Of course, teaching remains an essential duty. Students deserve clear instruction, useful feedback, and access to their instructors. However, giving research greater priority does not require professors to neglect teaching.

In conclusion, professors should remain active researchers throughout their academic careers and should generally devote more time to research than to teaching. Research keeps their expertise current, creates valuable opportunities for students, and produces discoveries that benefit society.

Visionary artists bring enjoyment to lives that can sometimes feel monotonous. Because art influences people, some people believe governments should restrict what artists may create. Personally, I firmly believe that artists should be free to express their thoughts and ideas, and broad government limits on creative work are unjust.

A common argument for regulation is that unrestricted art may spread misinformation and disturb society. However, audiences understand that novels, films, paintings, and performances often contain imagination, exaggeration, or complete fiction. Adults can also compare an artistic claim with other information before accepting it as true. A fictional film, for example, is normally understood as a story rather than a factual report. Broad censorship is therefore a poor answer to the fear of misinformation. If a work is clearly fictional, viewers can appreciate it without treating details as fact. If a work accurately reflects corruption, discrimination, or another unpleasant reality, suppressing it would simply hide a problem that deserves discussion.

A more serious concern arises when art contains disturbing themes such as violence, madness, explicit sexuality, or cruelty. Such material can be inappropriate for children who do not yet have the maturity to interpret it carefully. I therefore agree that reasonable limits on children's exposure to clearly adult material are justified. Age ratings and parental controls can protect younger audiences without banning a work for everyone.

When adults are the audience, however, difficult themes should not automatically be concealed. Mature viewers can decide whether they wish to watch, read, or avoid a particular work. Art that portrays violence or social conflict can also help adults think about problems that already exist. A serious film about domestic abuse, for instance, may be uncomfortable, but it can encourage discussion of an issue that is often hidden. Removing every disturbing subject would make art less capable of examining real human experience.

Broad government control also creates a danger because authorities may use vague ideas to suppress legitimate criticism. What one government calls offensive may simply be a viewpoint that challenges its policies. If artists fear punishment whenever they question powerful institutions, they will choose safer subjects and society will lose independent voices.

Artistic freedom also makes society more vibrant. Writers, filmmakers, musicians, and painters introduce new ideas that people may not encounter in ordinary routines. Their work can entertain, inspire, challenge assumptions, and help different communities share their experiences.

In conclusion, I do not support broad constraints on artists' creations. Reasonable safeguards can limit children's exposure to unsuitable material, but adults should remain free to judge artistic works for themselves. Governments should intervene only in narrow cases of direct and serious harm, not merely because a work is fictional, disturbing, or critical. Artists should be encouraged to share their creative ideas because the world benefits from the imagination and vibrancy they provide.

When choosing a place to live, public services strongly affect everyday comfort. My hometown provides most basic services reasonably well, but transportation remains frustrating. I face traffic jams almost every day, and the limited bus system makes many journeys difficult. Therefore, the improvement I want most in my community is a wider and more reliable public transportation system.

The first change should be to provide more types of public transportation, such as a subway or an elevated train. At present, buses are the only public transportation available in my area. When a bus is delayed or crowded, residents have no practical public alternative. Adding a subway or elevated train would give commuters another dependable way to reach important destinations. Rail services can follow fixed routes and published schedules that passengers can check before leaving home. A commuter could plan when to depart instead of simply waiting for the next bus. More transport choices would also reduce road congestion. If part of the population used trains instead of driving, fewer private cars would enter busy roads during rush hour.

The bus network itself also needs expansion. Only two bus routes currently serve my locality, so many destinations are not directly connected. If I want to visit a place outside those routes, I first have to travel to the central station and then transfer to another bus. This indirect journey can turn a short trip into a long one and waste valuable time. Adding routes that connect residential areas directly with schools, shopping areas, hospitals, and workplaces would make buses much more useful. Direct routes would reduce unnecessary transfers and shorten everyday journeys. They would also help elderly residents and students who may find repeated transfers difficult.

Better public transportation would also reduce dependence on private cars. Many residents drive because public transportation does not take them where they need to go conveniently. If buses and trains became frequent and well connected, some residents could leave their cars at home. Using fewer private cars can lower household expenses. Fuel prices are rising, and regular driving also brings parking and maintenance costs. Lower car use would also conserve energy resources. Every unnecessary car trip consumes fuel that could be saved when many passengers travel together on a bus or train.

Better transportation would also help residents who cannot afford a car or cannot drive. Reliable buses and trains would give them easier access to schools, jobs, shops, and medical services without depending on other people.

In conclusion, transportation is a fundamental service because it directly shapes people's daily lives. My hometown should expand bus routes and introduce additional options such as subways or elevated trains. These changes would save time, reduce congestion, lower dependence on private cars, and conserve fuel. I hope that improving public transportation will make travel easier for everyone in the community.

Taking a gap year before university has become increasingly common. Some students travel, while others work. In my view, taking a well-planned break before higher education is beneficial because it helps students become more independent, understand their goals, and prepare financially for university.

One major advantage is the personal growth that comes from real-world experience. Traveling to unfamiliar places forces students to solve practical problems on their own. These situations can build confidence and independence in ways that ordinary school routines do not. Work has a similar effect because students must follow schedules, cooperate with colleagues, and accept responsibility for their performance. As a result, students often return to education with greater maturity.

A gap year can also help students make better decisions about their future. Many school leavers must choose a university subject before they have experienced much outside the classroom. Working in an office, a shop, or another environment can show them what particular careers are actually like. These experiences may confirm an ambition or reveal that a planned career is not suitable. Making that discovery before beginning a degree can prevent students from wasting years and money on a course they do not truly want.

There are financial benefits as well for students who choose to work. A student who saves part of a year's earnings can use that money for tuition, books, rent, or daily expenses. Having savings can reduce pressure on the student's family and may allow the student to work less during the semester.

Of course, taking a break also involves risks. Once students begin earning a regular salary, some may be reluctant to give up financial independence and return to full-time study. Others may find it difficult to readjust to examinations and academic deadlines after a long absence. Some may even choose immediate employment instead of completing a university degree. However, these risks are strongest when the gap year has no clear purpose or end date. Students who set a return date and keep some connection with study are more likely to maintain their academic direction.

In conclusion, I support taking a break before commencing higher education when the year is used productively. Traveling and working can make students more mature, independent, financially prepared, and certain about their future choices. Although a gap year can make returning to study harder, careful planning can reduce that danger. A purposeful break can therefore help students enter university with greater confidence and contribute more effectively.
